page.title: Enhancing Blurry Club Recall
page.description: Applying state-of-the-art segmentation and a custom heuristic augmentation method to improve blurred club head detection without changing inference speed.
page.role: My role: I applied a state-of-the-art segmentation model, designed a heuristic method to synthesize motion-blurred clubs, and built the augmentation pipeline that improved detection on difficult footage.

banner.label: Golf swing pose and club detection

sections.title: Goal
paragraphs: Make club head detection more reliable under motion blur, especially in face-on footage and around impact, where rapid club movement makes detection difficult. These moments occupy only a small part of a swing but are critical for golf swing measurement.

The previous model could detect the club head in clearer frames but often missed it under blur. The goal was to improve recall across both high-quality footage and videos captured at lower frame rates or in poor lighting. Because missed detections were the larger practical problem, some loss of precision was considered acceptable.

sections.title: Challenges
paragraphs: Blurred club images accounted for only about 5% of the available data. Manually selecting these rare frames was slow and costly, and collecting more footage would produce the same imbalance.

I needed a practical way to turn the existing dataset into more useful training examples. The implementation challenge was to isolate the club, synthesize varied levels of blur, and filter out low-quality results so the augmented data remained useful for training.

sections.title: Contributions and Outcomes

metrics.label: Club head training examples after filtering

items: Applied state-of-the-art segmentation: I used a segmentation model to extract the club from existing frames, creating the components needed for targeted augmentation.

Designed a heuristic synthesis method: I developed a custom method to combine these components into motion-blurred club images. For each original frame, I generated three additional versions with mild, medium, and heavy blur to expand coverage of the failure cases.

Built the training-data pipeline: I generated the augmented examples and filtered out low-quality synthetic results. The resulting club head training data grew to at least twice its original size, using footage we already had.

Connected implementation to detection quality: Training with the augmented data enabled the final model to detect approximately 30% more difficult examples, with no substantial observed decrease in precision. The model architecture stayed the same, preserving inference speed.

subsections.title: A practical solution to a data bottleneck
paragraphs: I combined an available segmentation model with a task-specific heuristic method to address a concrete detector failure. This made it possible to expand rare blur cases from existing footage, reducing reliance on slow manual selection and additional data collection.

subsections.title: Improvement through training data
paragraphs: The main outcome was a more capable detector using the same architecture and inference budget. The observed improvement, with no substantial precision loss or observed overfitting, showed that the augmentation was useful for the difficult footage we evaluated.

subsections.title: A concrete next iteration
paragraphs: I would improve the synthesis pipeline by using an inpainting model to reconstruct the background where the original club was removed. Cleaner backgrounds could reduce compositing artifacts and make the augmented images more realistic.

sections.title: Results
paragraphs: The segmentation-guided augmentation pipeline enabled the final model to detect approximately 30% more difficult examples, with no substantial observed loss of precision. This improvement came from the training-data workflow while retaining the same model architecture and inference speed.
